title: fix(bash): keep excluded variables out of execution results
body:
## Problem

Callers use `Bash.exec(..., { replaceEnv: true })` to exclude constructor variables from an execution. Empty scripts, `exit`, and handled errors still returned those excluded variables in `result.env`, so forwarding or logging the result could expose values the caller deliberately removed.

For example, with constructor `SECRET=example-only`, `exec("exit", { env: {}, replaceEnv: true })` returned `result.env.SECRET === "example-only"`. It now returns an empty environment.

## Changes

Construct the effective execution environment before any early return or source-limit failure. Handled runtime errors return the live execution environment, retaining assignments made before the failure rather than restoring the initial values.

Results keep the existing null-prototype environment representation. Exit codes, diagnostics, output accounting, and normal merge semantics are preserved.

Command-scoped prefix bindings are unwound before returning a handled expansion failure. For `MARKER=kept; TEMP=secret echo ${MISSING:?required}`, `MARKER` survives while `TEMP` is removed or restored to its earlier value. Cleanup covers partial prefix-value processing as well as argument expansion, preserving actual `exit` and POSIX special-builtin binding behavior.

This is the result-contract follow-up identified in #439. That PR fixed nested-command inheritance; this change closes the separate return-path gap. Includes a patch changeset.

title: fix(jq): support array subtraction assignment and filtered deletion
body:
Fixes #266.

`.arr -= ["b"]` and `del(.arr[] | select(. == "b"))` currently leave `{"arr":["a","b","c"]}` unchanged. Both now return `{"arr":["a","c"]}`, as in jq, and `path(.arr[] | select(. == "b"))` returns `["arr",1]` instead of `[]`.

There were two root causes:

- `OP=` assignments now reuse the binary operators, so `-=` gets array subtraction. Array subtraction compares values structurally, ignoring object key order.
- `del` now uses the shared path collector instead of its own AST interpreter, and removes all selected paths from the original input in one pass, so multiple matches and duplicate or overlapping paths don't shift indexes. The collector follows paths through pipes, iteration, `select`, type filters, `if`, `//`, `try`, `label`, `as`, `first`, `limit`, `nth`, `getpath` and `recurse`. It yields paths lazily, so `first`, `limit` and `nth` stop early.

Behavior changes beyond the fix, all matching jq:

- Arithmetic assignments on unsupported operand types raise an error instead of assigning `null`.
- `del` raises an error for expressions that aren't paths, or for containers of the wrong type, instead of leaving the input unchanged.
- A postfix `?` suppresses errors only from its own access. `.a.b?` raises errors from `.a`, and errors from an index or slice bound are raised.
- `elif` is parsed as an `if` nested in the else branch, so a condition with several results or none selects branches like jq. Each `elif` counts toward the parser depth limit.
- `.a[.i]` reads `.i` from the input instead of from `.a`, as `path(.a[.i])` already did.

Error messages preview values like jq's `jv_dump_string_trunc`, serializing only what the preview shows. Previews, container comparisons and key enumeration are charged to the shared work and depth limits.

Tests: 200 comparison fixtures recorded against native jq 1.7.1; evaluator tests for input immutability, prototype-related keys, early stopping and work/depth/result limits; and six jq spec cases that now pass. Typecheck, lint, knip, and the jq, yq, query-engine, spec and comparison suites pass.

Out of scope: slice-path deletion, `delpaths`, and paths through user-defined functions or `reduce`/`foreach`. The lenient `path()`/`pick()` fallback for non-path expressions and the lenient `.[i]`/`.[]` reads on values of the wrong type are unchanged.
